# Organizations, Teams, and Decision Processes {#organizations-decisions}

On the night of 27 January 1986, engineers at a NASA contractor argued against
launching the space shuttle *Challenger* in record cold. The next morning the
shuttle broke apart 73 seconds after lift-off. Seventeen years later, a piece of
insulating foam struck the wing of *Columbia* during launch, engineers asked for
better imagery of the damage, and the request went nowhere. The official
investigation concluded that NASA's [organizational culture](#organizational-culture) and decision processes
were as much a cause of the second accident as the foam itself [@caib2003]. Both
tragedies involved talented people, abundant data, and formal review procedures.
Neither can be explained by individual incompetence. They are failures of
*organizing*: of how groups notice problems, interpret ambiguous signals, learn
from the past, and decide whether to speak up or press on.

This chapter assembles the theories that explain how decisions are actually made
inside organizations and teams, as opposed to how they should be made in a
textbook. We begin with two accounts of decision processes that depart sharply
from rational choice: the **[garbage can model](#garbage-can-model)** and **[escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment)**.
We then turn to how organizations accumulate and create knowledge
(**[organizational learning](#organizational-learning)** and **[knowledge creation](#knowledge-creation)**), to the shared
self-understandings and values that steer behaviour (**[organizational identity](#organizational-identity)**,
**organizational culture**, and **[paradox theory](#paradox-theory)**), to the interpersonal climate
of teams (**[psychological safety](#psychological-safety)**), to how the composition and social context of
the workforce shape attitudes (**[attraction-selection-attrition](#attraction-selection-attrition)** and **social
information processing**), and finally to **[sensemaking](#sensemaking)**, the process through
which people construct the situations they then act upon. Together these theories
form the core of the behavioural and interpretive tradition in organization
theory, a tradition that starts from the observation that organizations are
boundedly rational, socially constructed, and path dependent
[@cyert1963; @weick1979] (Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-glance)).

```{r od-tab-glance}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Theory, ~`Core question`, ~`Level of analysis`, ~`Key source`,
  "[Garbage can model](#garbage-can-model)", "How are choices made when goals, technology, and participation are all unclear?", "Organization", "Cohen, March & Olsen (1972)",
  "[Escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment)", "Why do decision makers keep investing in failing courses of action?", "Individual / group / organization", "Staw (1976)",
  "[Organizational learning](#organizational-learning)", "How do organizations encode experience into routines, and when do they question them?", "Organization", "Argyris & Schön (1978), Levitt & March (1988)",
  "[Knowledge creation](#knowledge-creation)", "How is new knowledge created through conversion of tacit and explicit knowledge?", "Individual to organization", "Nonaka (1994)",
  "[Organizational identity](#organizational-identity)", "Who are we as an organization, and how does that shape action?", "Organization", "Albert & Whetten (1985)",
  "[Organizational culture](#organizational-culture)", "What shared assumptions and values guide behaviour?", "Organization / group", "Schein (2010)",
  "[Paradox theory](#paradox-theory)", "How can organizations sustain contradictory demands over time?", "Individual / organization", "Smith & Lewis (2011)",
  "[Psychological safety](#psychological-safety)", "When do team members feel safe to speak up, admit errors, and learn?", "Team", "Edmondson (1999)",
  "[Attraction-selection-attrition](#attraction-selection-attrition)", "Why do organizations become homogeneous over time?", "Individual / organization", "Schneider (1987)",
  "[Social information processing](#social-information-processing)", "How do social cues shape job attitudes?", "Individual / workgroup", "Salancik & Pfeffer (1978)",

## Garbage Can Model {#garbage-can-model}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** In "organized anarchies", decisions are not the output of a
sequence that runs from problem to analysis to choice. They emerge when
independent streams of problems, solutions, participants, and choice
opportunities happen to meet. Timing and access, not intention, explain much of
what gets decided.

**Origins.** Organization theory and public administration. @cohen1972,
extending the behavioural theory of @cyert1963. Applied to public policy by
@kingdon1984.

**Level of analysis.** Organization (universities, government agencies,
professional firms, new ventures), and policy systems.

**Key constructs.** Problematic preferences, unclear technology, fluid
participation, problem stream, solution stream, participant stream, choice
opportunities, decision by resolution, oversight, and flight, load, access
structure.

**Boundary conditions.** Strongest when goals are inconsistent or ill-defined,
cause-effect knowledge is weak, and attention is scarce and shifting. Weaker in
tightly coupled, well-understood operational settings.

**Related theories.** [Behavioral theory of the firm](#behavioral-theory-of-the-firm) (Section \@ref(behavioral-theory-of-the-firm)),
[Attention-based view](#attention-based-view) (Section \@ref(attention-based-view)), [Bounded rationality](#bounded-rationality) (Section \@ref(bounded-rationality)),
[Sensemaking](#sensemaking).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@cohen1972 began with an empirical observation about universities. Their goals are
multiple and contested (**problematic preferences**), nobody fully understands
how teaching or research produce results (**unclear technology**), and faculty,
students, and administrators drift in and out of decisions depending on their
other commitments (**fluid participation**). The authors called such settings
**organized anarchies** and argued that standard models of choice, which assume
that problems precede and motivate solutions, describe them poorly.

Instead, an organization can be viewed as a collection of choices looking for
problems, issues and feelings looking for decision situations in which they might
be aired, solutions looking for issues to which they might be the answer, and
decision makers looking for work. Four relatively independent **streams** flow
through the organization. A **choice opportunity**, such as a budget meeting, a
hiring committee, or a strategic review, is the "garbage can" into which
participants dump whatever problems and solutions are currently active. What
comes out depends on the mix in the can at that moment.

The authors formalized the argument in a computer simulation and identified three
ways in which choices are made:

- **Resolution.** A choice resolves the problems attached to it, the classic
  rational pattern.
- **Oversight.** A choice is made quickly, before problems attach to it, so it
  resolves nothing that was not already settled.
- **Flight.** Problems attach to a choice, but the choice is delayed until the
  problems leave for another, more attractive choice opportunity. The choice is
  then made without resolving them.

A central result of the simulation was that resolution is *not* the dominant
style of decision making except when the load on the system is light. Under
heavy load, oversight and flight dominate, important problems are more likely to
remain unresolved, and decision makers spend much of their time on the same
problems in different arenas [@cohen1972].

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-garbage) shows the garbage can model: four loosely coupled streams meet in choice opportunities.

```{r od-fig-garbage, fig.cap = "The garbage can model: four loosely coupled streams meet in choice opportunities. Whether a choice resolves problems depends on timing, load, and access rules rather than on a planned problem-solving sequence. Based on Cohen, March & Olsen (1972)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  P  [label = "Problems\\n(issues, complaints,\\nperformance gaps)", %s]
  S  [label = "Solutions\\n(ideas, technologies,\\npet projects)", %s]
  A  [label = "Participants\\n(who has time\\nand access)", %s]
  C  [label = "Choice opportunity\\n(the garbage can:\\nmeeting, budget, review)", %s]
  R  [label = "Resolution", %s]
  O  [label = "Oversight", %s]
  F  [label = "Flight", %s]
  M  [label = "Organized anarchy\\nand system load", %s]
  P -> C
  S -> C
  A -> C
  C -> R
  C -> O
  C -> F
  M -> C [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism,
   node_outcome, node_outcome, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

The garbage can model does not claim that organizations are irrational. It claims
that **temporal coincidence** matters. A solution championed by a powerful
participant can wait years for a problem to which it can be attached, and a
problem that arrives when attention is elsewhere may be ignored even if it is
severe. @kingdon1984 adapted this idea to public policy as the **multiple streams
framework**: a policy change becomes likely when a problem stream, a policy
(solution) stream, and a political stream converge during a brief **policy
window**, often with help from a **policy entrepreneur** who couples them (Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-gcm)).

```{r od-tab-gcm}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Classic rational sequence`, ~`Garbage can account`, ~`Managerial implication`,
  "Problems are identified, then solutions are sought", "Solutions often exist first and search for problems", "Track which solutions are being promoted, not only which problems exist",
  "Goals are clear and stable", "Preferences are discovered through action", "Expect goals to be rationalised after the fact",
  "Participants are fixed", "Participation depends on time, energy, and other arenas", "Agenda and attendance shape outcomes as much as arguments",
  "Choices resolve problems", "Many choices are made by oversight or flight", "Audit whether decisions actually closed the issues they were meant to address",
  "Timing is incidental", "Timing and coincidence are central", "Prepare solutions in advance and act when windows open"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Rational choice versus the garbage can account of organizational decisions.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The original article was a thought experiment illustrated by simulation, and its
empirical support comes mostly from qualitative studies of universities, public
agencies, and policy making. Kingdon's interview-based study of United States
federal policy agendas is the most influential application [@kingdon1984]. The
model also influenced work on attention allocation and organizational routines,
including the [attention-based view](#attention-based-view) (Section \@ref(attention-based-view)).

::: {.debate}
**Does the simulation match the theory?** @bendor2001 offered the sharpest
critique. They argued that the computer model implements a far more structured
organization than the verbal theory describes (for example, access rules and
energy loads are fixed by design), that individual agency disappears from the
model, and that several of the verbal claims do not follow from the simulation.
Defenders reply that the garbage can is best read as a sensitizing metaphor about
loose coupling and timing, not as a precise predictive model. A second
limitation is falsifiability: almost any decision outcome can be narrated as the
product of colliding streams, so researchers need to specify ex ante which stream
configurations should produce which outcomes.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: the technology looking for a problem.** A retailer's
analytics team has built a sophisticated recommendation engine. No business unit
asked for it. For two years it is presented at quarterly planning meetings
without adoption. Then a sharp drop in online conversion coincides with a new
chief digital officer's arrival and an open budget cycle. Within weeks the engine
is funded as "the answer" to conversion, although nobody has diagnosed why
conversion fell. The garbage can lens explains the timing and warns about the
risk: the problem may not be the one the solution solves. A practical response is
to separate the *window* (the moment of attention) from the *diagnosis* by
requiring a short root-cause analysis before any solution already in the pipeline
is attached to a newly salient problem.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* The probability that a pre-existing internal proposal is adopted rises
  sharply in periods following an exogenous performance shock, independent of the
  proposal's fit with the shock.
- *H2.* Under high decision load (many concurrent choice opportunities), a larger
  share of decisions will be recorded without resolution of the issues raised in
  meeting minutes.

**Designs and data.** Meeting minutes and board agendas coded for problems,
solutions, and attendance. Event-history models of proposal adoption. Agent-based
simulation that explicitly varies access structures. Policy-agenda datasets for
public-sector applications.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Using the garbage can as an all-purpose excuse.** Calling a decision process a
"garbage can" explains nothing unless the analyst shows that the streams were in
fact independent and that timing, rather than deliberate choice, determined the
outcome. The model is a description of particular conditions (organized anarchy
and high load), not a general claim that organizations are chaotic.
:::

## Escalation of Commitment {#escalation-of-commitment}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Decision makers who are responsible for a course of action tend to
continue, and even increase, investment in it after receiving negative feedback,
beyond the point that a forward-looking analysis would justify.

**Origins.** Organizational behaviour and social psychology. @staw1976, with the
theoretical framework of @staw1981. The related **sunk cost effect** was
documented by @arkes1985.

**Level of analysis.** Individual, group, and organization (projects, product
lines, acquisitions, public programmes).

**Key constructs.** Sunk costs, personal responsibility, self-justification,
negative feedback, project completion, framing of losses, public commitment,
de-escalation.

**Boundary conditions.** Requires a prior decision, ambiguous or negative feedback,
and an opportunity to reinvest. Effects are weaker when decision makers are not
responsible for the initial choice, when the cost of continuation is salient, and
when exit is institutionally easy.

**Related theories.** [Cognitive dissonance](#cognitive-dissonance-theory) (Section \@ref(cognitive-dissonance-theory)),
[Prospect theory](#prospect-theory-overview) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-overview)), [Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)),
[Agency theory](#agency-theory) (Section \@ref(agency-theory)), [Real options](#real-options-theory) (Section \@ref(real-options-theory)),
[Groupthink](#groupthink) (Section \@ref(groupthink)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The title of Staw's 1976 article, "Knee-deep in the big muddy", alludes to a
Vietnam-era protest song, and the war itself, in which the United States
government repeatedly increased its commitment in the face of discouraging
results, was a motivating example. @staw1976 tested the underlying idea in a role-playing experiment. Business
students acting as a corporate financial officer allocated research and
development funds to one of two divisions, then learned how the division had
performed, then allocated a second round of funds. Participants who had
personally chosen the initial division and then learned it had performed poorly
allocated significantly more money to it in the second round than participants
who had not made the original choice. Responsibility for a losing decision
produced more, not less, investment in it.

@staw1981 interpreted the finding through **self-justification**: people are
motivated to demonstrate, to themselves and others, that an earlier decision was
correct. Reinvesting keeps open the possibility that the decision will be
vindicated. Admitting failure closes it. Four years later, @arkes1985 documented
the closely related **sunk cost effect**, the tendency to continue an endeavour
once an investment of money, effort, or time has been made. In one of their field
studies, theatre patrons who had been randomly assigned to pay full price for
season tickets attended more performances in the first part of the season than
patrons who had received discounts, although the money was spent either way.

The biologist Richard Dawkins and a colleague had independently named the error
the **Concorde fallacy**, after the Anglo-French supersonic airliner whose
development continued despite mounting evidence that it would not be a
commercial success [@dawkins1976]. @arkes1999 reviewed the animal and human
evidence and argued that the effect is distinctively human, rooted in an
overgeneralised rule against wasting resources.

### Core logic and propositions

Escalation is an error only relative to a normative benchmark. In rational
choice, past costs are **sunk**: they cannot be recovered whatever one does next,
so they should not influence a forward-looking decision. The right question is
always whether the *incremental* cost of continuing is justified by the
*incremental* expected value. Escalation occurs when sunk costs, prior
commitments, or identity concerns enter that comparison. Building on
@staw1981, @brockner1992, and the meta-analysis of @sleesman2012, the theory can
be summarised in propositions:

- **P1 (Responsibility).** Decision makers who are personally responsible for an
  initial decision escalate more after negative feedback than decision makers who
  inherit it.
- **P2 (Sunk costs).** The larger the prior investment, the greater the
  willingness to continue, holding forward-looking prospects constant.
- **P3 (Loss framing).** Because continuing offers a chance to avoid a certain
  loss, decision makers in the loss domain take the risky option of
  continuation, consistent with [prospect theory](#prospect-theory-overview) (Section \@ref(prospect-theory-overview)).
- **P4 (Completion).** Willingness to continue rises as a project approaches
  completion, even when the remaining cost exceeds the remaining value.
- **P5 (Structural and social binding).** Public commitment, political support,
  and institutionalised projects make exit costly for the organization, even
  after individual decision makers have lost confidence.

Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-escalation) illustrates the economic logic with a
stylised project. The value of completion is fixed. Each quarter, the estimate of
the cost still required to finish rises. A forward-looking decision maker exits
once the remaining cost exceeds the remaining value. An escalating decision maker,
anchored on what has already been spent, continues long after that point.

```{r od-fig-escalation, fig.cap = "Stylised escalation of commitment. The rational exit point is where the estimated cost to complete first exceeds the value of completion. Funds spent after that point (shaded) represent escalation. Illustrative numbers only.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1976)
q <- 1:12
value_complete <- 100                                       # value if the project is finished
remaining <- 40 * 1.16^(q - 1) + rnorm(12, 0, 2)              # cost-to-complete estimate keeps rising
spent <- cumsum(c(0, rep(18, 11)))                            # cumulative spending each quarter
proj <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(q, value = remaining, series = "Estimated cost to complete"),
  data.frame(q, value = spent, series = "Cumulative spending (sunk)")
)
exit_q <- min(q[remaining > value_complete])
ggplot(proj, aes(q, value, colour = series)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = exit_q, xmax = 12, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = pal[["orange"]], alpha = 0.08) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = value_complete, linetype = "dashed", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = exit_q, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = value_complete + 8, label = "Value of completing the project", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = exit_q + 0.15, y = 75, label = "Forward-looking\nexit point", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.3, colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  annotate("text", x = 10.4, y = 20, label = "Escalation zone", size = 3.5, fontface = "bold",
           colour = ink[["primary"]]) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Estimated cost to complete" = pal[["blue"]],
                                 "Cumulative spending (sunk)" = pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:12) +
  labs(x = "Quarter since project launch", y = "Money (index)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Sunk costs should not enter the continuation decision",
       caption = "Stylised simulation. Continue only while the cost to complete is below the value of completion.")
```

### Determinants of escalation

@ross1993 organized the many determinants of escalation into four classes, a
framework that later reviews retained [@sleesman2012; @sleesman2018] (Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-escalation)).

```{r od-tab-escalation}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Class of determinant`, ~Examples, ~`Theoretical root`, ~`De-escalation lever`,
  "Project", "Ambiguous feedback, large payoff on completion, long time horizons, closeness to completion", "Expected value, information economics", "Pre-set milestones and kill criteria tied to forward-looking value",
  "Psychological", "Personal responsibility, self-justification, loss framing, sunk cost reasoning", "Dissonance, prospect theory", "Rotate decision makers and separate initial and continuation decisions",
  "Social", "Public commitment, face-saving, norms of consistency for leaders", "Impression management", "Reward accurate early reporting of bad news",
  "Structural", "Political coalitions, institutionalised projects, side bets, sunk investments in people and assets", "Institutional theory, resource dependence", "Independent review boards and staged funding"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Determinants of escalation of commitment, organized following Ross and Staw (1993).")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The phenomenon is well supported. @sleesman2012 meta-analysed escalation research
and confirmed that sunk costs, personal responsibility, and project-related
factors such as proximity to completion predict continued commitment, while
showing that effect sizes vary considerably across settings. Field studies trace
escalation in nuclear power, information systems, banking, and professional
sports. @ross1993 reconstructed the history of the Shoreham nuclear power plant on
Long Island, whose cost estimates rose from tens of millions to billions of
dollars over two decades, and which was completed but never entered commercial
operation. They showed how project, psychological, social, and structural forces
dominated at different stages: early commitment was driven by projected
economics, later commitment by political and structural binding. In information
systems, @keil2000 surveyed audit professionals about runaway software projects
and compared four explanations (self-justification, [prospect theory](#prospect-theory) (Chapter \@ref(prospect-theory)), agency
theory, and approach-avoidance theory), finding that several of them contributed
to explaining escalation.

::: {.debate}
**Error or rational persistence?** Not every decision to continue is escalation.
Persistence can be rational when feedback is noisy, when early losses are
expected in innovation, or when reputational benefits of consistency are real.
Critics note that many laboratory designs make it impossible to tell whether
participants are biased or are updating sensibly on ambiguous information.
Case labels can also oversimplify. The Concorde programme was governed by an
Anglo-French intergovernmental agreement that made unilateral cancellation
diplomatically costly, a structural rather than a purely psychological driver
of continuation. The
theoretical frontier, reviewed by @sleesman2018, is a multilevel account that
separates individual biases from team and organizational forces and studies
**de-escalation** as a process in its own right.
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Large IT programmes.** Enterprise software and public-sector IT projects are
the modern home of escalation research because they combine long horizons,
ambiguous progress measures, and highly visible sponsors. The United Kingdom's
National Programme for IT in the National Health Service, launched in 2002 and
dismantled in 2011 after sustained criticism from parliamentary committees and
the National Audit Office, is a widely discussed public example. Research on such
projects [@keil2000] suggests three practical safeguards: **stage-gated funding**
that requires a fresh forward-looking business case at each gate, **separation
of roles** so that the sponsor who initiated a project does not alone decide
whether it continues, and **pre-registered kill criteria** written when the
project is launched and the sponsor's ego is not yet invested.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Venture capital and real options.** Venture investors explicitly structure
funding in stages, so that each round is a new decision about the incremental
investment. In principle, staging converts a single large commitment into a
sequence of [real options](#real-options-theory) (Section \@ref(real-options-theory)). In practice, escalation can
reappear through follow-on investments made to protect earlier positions. Many
funds therefore have partners other than the original sponsor evaluate follow-on
rounds.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Executives who championed an acquisition will be less likely to divest
  the acquired unit after poor performance than successor executives, controlling
  for unit performance.
- *H2.* The positive effect of cumulative project spending on continuation will be
  weaker when funding is staged and continuation decisions are made by an
  independent committee.
- *H3.* Proximity to completion will increase continuation more strongly when
  progress is measured by spending than when it is measured by delivered
  functionality.

**Designs.** The classic two-stage allocation experiment [@staw1976] remains the
workhorse. Field designs exploit executive turnover as a shift in personal
responsibility, compare initiators and successors, or use project-level data
from IT portfolios, pharmaceutical pipelines, and sports drafts.

**Measures.** Additional resources allocated after negative feedback, time to
project termination, responsibility (initiator versus successor), sunk cost
magnitude, and proximity to completion.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Labelling every failed persistence as bias.** Escalation is defined relative to
a forward-looking benchmark. To claim escalation, researchers and managers need
to show that the information available at the time implied that continuation had
negative incremental expected value. Hindsight makes this look easier than it
was. Conversely, managers who quote "sunk costs are sunk" to kill every
struggling innovation project risk the opposite error of premature abandonment.
:::

## Organizational Learning {#organizational-learning}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Organizations learn by encoding inferences from experience into
routines that guide behaviour. Most learning refines existing routines
(single-loop), while deeper learning questions the goals and assumptions behind
them (double-loop).

**Origins.** Organization theory and the behavioural theory of the firm.
@argyris1978, @levitt1988, @huber1991, and the learning-curve tradition
summarised by @argote1990.

**Level of analysis.** Organization, with links to teams and individuals.

**Key constructs.** Routines, single-loop and double-loop learning, theories in
use versus espoused theories, knowledge acquisition, information distribution,
interpretation, organizational memory, learning curves, knowledge depreciation
and transfer, competency traps, superstitious learning.

**Boundary conditions.** Learning requires feedback that can be observed and
attributed. Learning is weaker when experience is rare, outcomes are noisy, or
cause and effect are separated in time.

**Related theories.** [Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)),
[Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)),
[Dynamic capabilities](#dynamic-capabilities-framework) (Section \@ref(dynamic-capabilities-framework)),
[Behavioral theory of the firm](#behavioral-theory-of-the-firm) (Section \@ref(behavioral-theory-of-the-firm)),
[Psychological safety](#psychological-safety).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

Three intellectual lines converge in organizational learning theory. The first
is the **behavioural theory of the firm**, in which organizations adapt their
goals, attention, and search rules in response to experience [@cyert1963]. The
second is the action-science tradition of @argyris1978, which focused on the gap
between what managers say they believe and what their behaviour reveals. The
third is the economics and engineering literature on **learning curves**, dating
back to the observation that the labour required to build an airframe falls
predictably as cumulative production rises [@wright1936].

@levitt1988 synthesised the first line in an influential review. Organizational
learning, they argued, is **routine-based**, **history-dependent**, and
**target-oriented**. Organizations encode inferences from history into routines
(rules, procedures, technologies, conventions) that persist even as personnel
change. Routines are adjusted when performance falls short of aspirations.
@huber1991 then mapped four constructs that organize the field: **knowledge
acquisition**, **information distribution**, **information interpretation**, and
**organizational memory**. @fiol1985 distinguished lower-level learning, which
adjusts behaviour within existing rules, from higher-level learning, which
changes the rules themselves.

### Core logic: single-loop and double-loop learning

@argyris1976 and @argyris1978 distinguished two kinds of learning. In
**single-loop learning**, an organization detects an error and corrects it by
changing its action strategy while leaving its governing values intact, much as a
thermostat adjusts heating to hold a set temperature. In **double-loop learning**,
the organization questions the governing variables themselves: it asks whether
the target temperature is right. Argyris and Schön also distinguished **espoused
theories** (what people say guides their action) from **theories in use**
(what their behaviour reveals). They argued that defensive routines, designed to
avoid embarrassment or threat, systematically block double-loop learning (Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-loops)).

```{r od-fig-loops, fig.cap = "Single-loop and double-loop learning. Single-loop learning changes action strategies to close a gap between consequences and governing variables. Double-loop learning questions the governing variables themselves. Based on Argyris and Schön (1978)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  G [label = "Governing variables\\n(goals, values,\\nassumptions)", %s]
  A [label = "Action strategies\\n(routines, plans,\\ntechniques)", %s]
  C [label = "Consequences\\n(match or\\nmismatch)", %s]
  G -> A -> C
  C -> A [label = " single loop", constraint = false, style = dashed]
  C -> G [label = " double loop", constraint = false, style = dashed, color = "#eb6834", fontcolor = "#eb6834"]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_outcome))
```

Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-loops) presents the single-loop versus double-loop learning.

```{r od-tab-loops}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Single-loop learning`, ~`Double-loop learning`,
  "Question asked", "Are we doing things right?", "Are we doing the right things?",
  "What changes", "Action strategies and routines", "Goals, norms, and underlying assumptions",
  "Typical trigger", "Performance below target", "Repeated failure, crisis, or new framing",
  "Typical method", "Process improvement, root-cause fixes", "Reframing, strategic review, surfacing assumptions",
  "Main obstacle", "Weak feedback or poor measurement", "Defensive routines that make assumptions undiscussable",
  "Related idea", "Exploitation", "Exploration"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Single-loop versus double-loop learning.")
```

### Learning curves: experience, transfer, and forgetting

The quantitative heart of the field is the **learning curve**: unit cost or
labour hours fall as a power function of cumulative output. @wright1936 observed
this regularity in aircraft manufacturing. @argote1990 reviewed evidence from
many industries and drew three conclusions that transformed the learning curve
from an engineering rule of thumb into an organizational theory. First, **rates
of learning vary dramatically across organizations**, even those producing the
same product. Second, **knowledge depreciates**: it decays when production is
interrupted or staff turn over. Third, **knowledge transfers** across units, but
imperfectly. @darr1995 showed these patterns in pizza franchises: stores learned
from cumulative experience, knowledge transferred across stores owned by the same
franchisee but not across stores with different owners, and acquired knowledge
depreciated quickly (Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-learning)).

```{r od-fig-learning, fig.cap = "Stylised learning curves. Unit cost falls with cumulative output, but organizations learn at different rates, and an interruption causes knowledge to depreciate. Axes are logarithmic, so a constant learning rate appears as a straight line. Illustrative numbers only.", fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(1990)
n <- unique(round(10^seq(0, 3, length.out = 60)))
curve_fn <- function(ratio) 100 * n^(log2(ratio))             # progress ratio: cost multiplier per doubling
fast <- curve_fn(0.80)
slow <- curve_fn(0.90)
dep <- fast
dep[n > 100] <- 100 * (pmax(n[n > 100] - 90, 1))^(log2(0.80))
lc <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(n, cost = fast * exp(rnorm(length(n), 0, 0.02)), plant = "Plant A: 80% progress ratio"),
  data.frame(n, cost = slow * exp(rnorm(length(n), 0, 0.02)), plant = "Plant B: 90% progress ratio"),
  data.frame(n, cost = dep * exp(rnorm(length(n), 0, 0.02)), plant = "Plant A with interruption at 100 units")
)
lc$plant <- factor(lc$plant, levels = c("Plant A: 80% progress ratio", "Plant B: 90% progress ratio",
                                        "Plant A with interruption at 100 units"))
ggplot(lc, aes(n, cost, colour = plant)) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]])) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Cumulative units produced (log scale)", y = "Unit cost (log scale, first unit = 100)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Organizations learn at different rates and also forget",
       caption = "Stylised curves. A progress ratio of 80% means unit cost falls 20% with each doubling of output.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

Learning-curve heterogeneity is now well documented in manufacturing, services,
and medicine. @pisano2001 found large differences across hospitals in how quickly
surgical teams improved after adopting a new minimally invasive cardiac
procedure, and @edmondson2001 traced the differences to team learning practices,
including whether team members felt able to speak up. Research on failure shows
that organizations often learn more from failures than from successes: in the
global orbital launch vehicle industry, @madsen2010 found that knowledge from
failures was retained longer than knowledge from successes. @haunschild2002 found
that airlines learned more from accidents and incidents with heterogeneous
causes, which force broader search. @argote2011 offer an integrative framework in
which experience interacts with organizational context to create knowledge that
is embedded in members, tools, and routines.

::: {.debate}
**The dark side of learning.** Learning can be myopic. @levinthal1993 argued that
organizations overweight the short run, the near neighbourhood, and success, so
that learning itself drives out exploration. @levitt1988 described **competency
traps**, in which favourable performance with an inferior routine leads the
organization to accumulate more experience with it, making a superior routine
unattractive to try, and **superstitious learning**, in which the link between
action and outcome is misread. Others question whether "organizations" learn at
all, or whether the construct is simply the aggregation of individual learning.
Most contemporary scholars locate organizational learning in changes to
routines, tools, and transactive memory that persist when individuals leave
[@argote2011].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Toyota and learning as an operating system.** The Toyota Production System is
widely studied as an organization designed for continuous single-loop learning
on the shop floor. @spear1999 argued that its distinctive feature is not any
particular tool but a set of tacit rules that make every activity, connection,
and flow a structured hypothesis that can be tested. Problems are surfaced
immediately (for example, by stopping the line), and countermeasures are
developed by the people closest to the work. Taiichi Ohno's practice of asking
"why" repeatedly until a root cause is reached is a disciplined form of
problem-oriented search [@ohno1988]. The system also illustrates the limits of
transfer: many firms copied visible tools such as kanban cards without the
learning routines behind them, and saw smaller gains.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Learning from failure in safety-critical industries.** Commercial aviation's
incident reporting systems, which protect reporters who disclose their own near
misses, are an institutional design for converting rare and costly failures into
shared knowledge. Research on airlines and launch vehicles suggests that such
systems work best when they encourage analysis of diverse causes rather than
single-cause attributions [@haunschild2002; @madsen2010]. @cannon2005 argue that
most organizations fail to learn from failure because of social and technical
barriers to identifying, analysing, and deliberately experimenting with failure,
and propose a sequence of practices to overcome each barrier.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Production units with higher rates of team learning behaviour will show
  steeper learning curves for a newly introduced product.
- *H2.* Knowledge depreciation (the loss of productivity after a production gap)
  will be smaller in units with codified routines than in units relying on
  individual expertise.
- *H3.* Organizations learn more from failures with heterogeneous causes than
  from failures with a single dominant cause.

**Designs and data.** Learning-curve regressions of unit cost or quality on
cumulative experience with depreciation parameters [@argote1990; @darr1995].
Panel data on accidents, recalls, or surgical outcomes. Ethnographies of
routines. Field experiments that vary after-action reviews.

**Measures.** Cumulative output, progress ratio, depreciation rate, transfer
across units, frequency of after-action reviews, changes in codified procedures.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Equating learning with improvement.** Organizations can learn the wrong lessons.
A measured fall in errors may reflect less reporting rather than fewer errors,
and success can teach complacency. Studies should separate changes in knowledge
(routines, cognition) from changes in performance and test whether the
experience-performance link runs through the proposed knowledge mechanism.
:::

## Knowledge Creation {#knowledge-creation}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Organizations create new knowledge through a continuous dialogue
between **tacit** and **explicit** knowledge, captured in four modes of
conversion (socialization, externalization, combination, internalization) that
spiral from individuals to groups to the whole organization.

**Origins.** Management and Japanese innovation studies. @nonaka1994 and
@nonaka1995, building on Polanyi's concept of tacit knowledge [@polanyi1966].

**Level of analysis.** Individual, group, organization, and interorganizational
networks.

**Key constructs.** Tacit and explicit knowledge, SECI modes, knowledge spiral,
redundancy, requisite variety, middle-up-down management.

**Boundary conditions.** Most relevant for product development and
knowledge-intensive work in which much know-how cannot be written down.
Cultural and organizational context shapes the ease of socialization.

**Related theories.** [Knowledge-based view](#knowledge-based-view) (Section \@ref(knowledge-based-view)),
[Absorptive capacity](#absorptive-capacity) (Section \@ref(absorptive-capacity)),
[Organizational learning](#organizational-learning).
:::

### Core logic

@polanyi1966 observed that people know more than they can tell. Such **tacit
knowledge** (the feel of a skilled baker's hands, the judgement of an experienced
engineer) is personal, context specific, and hard to formalize. **Explicit
knowledge** can be codified in documents, formulas, and databases. Organizational
learning theory tended to treat organizations as processors of information.
@nonaka1994 argued instead that the core of innovation is the *creation* of new
knowledge, and that it happens when tacit and explicit knowledge are converted
into one another. The four modes form the **SECI** model shown in Figure
\@ref(fig:od-fig-seci).

```{r od-fig-seci, fig.cap = "The SECI model of knowledge creation. Knowledge moves through four modes of conversion and spirals outward from individuals to groups, the organization, and partners. Based on Nonaka (1994) and Nonaka and Takeuchi (1995).", fig.height = 4.6}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  S [label = "Socialization\\ntacit to tacit\\n(apprenticeship, shared experience)", %s]
  E [label = "Externalization\\ntacit to explicit\\n(metaphor, concept, prototype)", %s]
  C [label = "Combination\\nexplicit to explicit\\n(documents, databases, specs)", %s]
  I [label = "Internalization\\nexplicit to tacit\\n(learning by doing)", %s]
  L [label = "Knowledge spiral:\\nindividual, group,\\norganization, network", %s]
  {rank = same; S; E}
  {rank = same; I; C}
  S -> E
  E -> C
  C -> I
  I -> S
  L -> E [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_construct, node_outcome, node_moderator), rankdir = "TB", height = 440)
```

Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-seci) presents the four modes of knowledge conversion.

```{r od-tab-seci}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Mode, ~Conversion, ~`Typical practices`, ~`Business example`,
  "Socialization", "Tacit to tacit", "Apprenticeship, job rotation, site visits, working side by side", "A new engineer shadows a senior field technician",
  "Externalization", "Tacit to explicit", "Metaphors, analogies, concept papers, prototypes", "A design team turns a customer frustration into a product concept",
  "Combination", "Explicit to explicit", "Reports, specifications, knowledge bases, training manuals", "Merging test results into a standard operating procedure",
  "Internalization", "Explicit to tacit", "Simulation, practice, learning by doing", "Staff practise a new procedure until it becomes routine"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "The four modes of knowledge conversion.")
```

@nonaka1995 illustrated the model with Japanese product development cases. The
best-known is the development of an automatic home bread-making machine at
Matsushita in the 1980s. Early prototypes produced poor bread, so a software
developer trained alongside the head baker at a leading Osaka hotel to absorb
his kneading technique (socialization), and the team then translated what she
had learned into a design specification for the machine (externalization). The
authors also emphasised organizational conditions that enable the spiral,
including intention, autonomy, creative chaos, redundancy of information, and
requisite variety, and argued for **middle-up-down** management in which middle
managers translate top management's vision into concepts that front-line teams
can work with.

::: {.debate}
**Is tacit knowledge convertible at all?** The most persistent critique concerns
externalization. Following Polanyi, some scholars argue that tacit knowledge is by
definition inexpressible, so it cannot be "converted" into explicit form, only
supported or demonstrated. @gourlay2006 questioned the empirical basis of the
model and whether the four modes are distinct processes. @nonaka2009 responded by
clarifying that tacit and explicit knowledge lie on a continuum and that
conversion is a social process of articulation, not a literal transfer. A second
critique is cultural: the model was developed from Japanese cases, and its
assumptions about long tenure and dense socialization may not transfer to
organizations with high turnover and contractual employment.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: capturing field know-how.** An industrial equipment
company finds that its best service technicians fix faults in half the time of
others, but its manuals do not explain why. A knowledge-creation approach would
not start with a database. It would pair junior and senior technicians on
difficult jobs (socialization), hold structured debriefs in which experts explain
their diagnostic hunches through analogies (externalization), consolidate the
debriefs into decision trees embedded in the service app (combination), and use
simulated faults in training (internalization). The spiral then repeats as the
decision trees are tested in the field.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Designs and measures.** Survey scales for the four SECI modes, case studies of
product development, network analysis of knowledge flows, and studies of
knowledge codification and its effects on transfer. Hypotheses typically link
the intensity of particular modes to innovation outcomes (for example, that
externalization practices predict new product concept quality more strongly
than combination practices do).
:::

## Organizational Identity {#organizational-identity}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Organizational members share beliefs about what is central,
enduring, and distinctive about their organization. These beliefs filter how
issues are interpreted, which actions feel legitimate, and how members respond to
outside images that conflict with them.

**Origins.** Organization theory. @albert1985, with major empirical work by
@dutton1991 and the social identity foundation of @ashforth1989.

**Level of analysis.** Organization (collective identity) and individual
(organizational identification).

**Key constructs.** Central, enduring, and distinctive attributes, organizational
identification, construed external image, reputation, identity threat, adaptive
instability.

**Boundary conditions.** Identity matters most when issues are ambiguous and when
members identify strongly. In loosely coupled or newly formed organizations,
identity claims may be weakly shared.

**Related theories.** [Social identity theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)),
[Organizational culture](#organizational-culture), [Legitimacy](#legitimacy) (Section \@ref(legitimacy)),
[Optimal distinctiveness](#optimal-distinctiveness-theory) (Section \@ref(optimal-distinctiveness-theory)).
:::

### Core logic

@albert1985 proposed that an organization's identity consists of members'
self-referential claims about what is **central** to the organization, what is
**enduring** about it over time, and what is **distinctive** compared with
similar organizations. Identity questions ("Who are we?") become salient at
critical junctures such as founding, loss of a sustaining resource, mergers,
rapid growth, or retrenchment. @whetten2006 later sharpened the concept, arguing
that identity claims are most visible when organizations face "fork in the road"
choices that would commit them to one self-definition over another.

At the individual level, @ashforth1989 applied [social identity
theory](#social-identity-theory) (Section \@ref(social-identity-theory)) to organizations. **Organizational
identification** is the perception of oneness with or belongingness to an
organization. When people identify strongly, the organization's successes and
failures feel personal, which motivates effort and loyalty but also defensiveness
when the organization is criticised (Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-identity)).

```{r od-tab-identity}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Concept, ~`Core question`, ~`Whose view`, ~`Example measure`,
  "Organizational identity", "Who do we believe we are?", "Members about the organization", "Members' ratings of central, enduring, and distinctive attributes",
  "Organizational identification", "How much is the organization part of who I am?", "Individual member", "Identification scale items on oneness with the organization",
  "Construed external image", "What do outsiders think of us, in our view?", "Members about outsiders' views", "Members' beliefs about how the public sees the firm",
  "Reputation", "What do outsiders actually think of us?", "External stakeholders", "Rankings, media tone, stakeholder surveys",
  "Organizational culture", "How do we do things here, and why?", "Members, often tacit", "Value profiles, observed practices, underlying assumptions"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Organizational identity and neighbouring concepts.")
```

### Evidence and extensions

@dutton1991 provided the field's foundational case study. In the 1980s the Port
Authority of New York and New Jersey faced a growing number of homeless people in
its bus terminal, train stations, and airports. The agency's members saw it as a
professional, technically excellent transportation organization, not a social
service agency, and they initially treated homelessness as a policing and
facilities problem. As media coverage and public criticism damaged the agency's
**construed external image**, members felt the gap between how they saw
themselves and how they believed outsiders saw them. That discomfort helped push
the agency to reframe the issue and invest in more humane and collaborative
responses. Identity and image, the authors argued, act as a mirror that shapes
how organizations interpret and respond to issues.

@elsbach1996 found a similar dynamic when *Business Week* rankings of business
schools threatened members' perceptions of their schools. Members responded by
highlighting alternative comparison categories and dimensions on which their
school excelled. @gioia2000 challenged the assumption that identity is enduring,
proposing **adaptive instability**: identity labels may stay constant while their
meanings shift as members reinterpret them in light of changing images.
@tripsas2009 showed how a firm's identity as a "digital photography company" made
it difficult to pursue opportunities that technology made possible but that did
not fit that identity, complementing the cognitive account of Polaroid's
difficulties in digital imaging in @tripsas2000.

::: {.debate}
**Enduring or fluid?** The original definition required identity to be enduring,
but empirical work repeatedly shows identity claims changing in response to
image, strategy, and leadership. Social-actor perspectives treat identity as
institutional claims that change slowly. Social-constructionist perspectives
treat identity as shared understandings that are continually renegotiated.
@whetten2006 defends a narrower definition to keep the concept distinct from
culture and image. A second debate concerns measurement: identity is easily
conflated with culture or reputation, and many studies infer identity from
self-presentation materials that may be impression management rather than
belief.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Identity in strategic change.** Firms that redefine their business often
discover that identity, not capability, is the binding constraint. When a
company that has seen itself as a hardware manufacturer moves to services or
software subscriptions, engineers may resist work that feels peripheral to "who
we are". Effective leaders in such transitions tend to reinterpret existing
identity labels rather than discard them (for example, moving from "we build
the best machines" to "we keep our customers' operations running"), which is the
adaptive instability that @gioia2000 describe.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Firms whose stated identity claims are inconsistent with a new strategic
  initiative will adopt it more slowly, controlling for capabilities.
- *H2.* Negative media coverage that conflicts with members' identity beliefs will
  trigger more issue-reframing activity than negative coverage that is consistent
  with those beliefs.

**Designs and data.** Longitudinal case studies with interviews and archival
documents. Text analysis of letters to shareholders, mission statements, and
internal communications. Survey measures of organizational identification.
Event studies of identity threats such as rankings or scandals.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Treating the mission statement as the identity.** Formal statements are
identity *claims*, often written for external audiences. Identity theory concerns
what members actually believe is central and distinctive. Valid studies
triangulate official claims with members' own accounts and with choices made at
identity-relevant forks in the road.
:::

## Organizational Culture {#organizational-culture}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Organizations develop shared, largely taken-for-granted
assumptions, learned as the group solved problems of external adaptation and
internal integration. These assumptions are expressed in espoused values and
visible artifacts, and they shape behaviour more powerfully than formal
structures.

**Origins.** Organizational psychology and anthropology. @schein2010 (first
edition 1985) and @schein1990. Quantitative measurement through the
Organizational Culture Profile of @oreilly1991.

**Level of analysis.** Organization and subgroups (functions, units,
professions).

**Key constructs.** Artifacts, espoused beliefs and values, basic underlying
assumptions, culture strength (intensity and consensus), culture content,
subcultures, person-culture fit.

**Boundary conditions.** Culture is most consequential where formal controls are
incomplete and behaviour cannot be fully specified. Culture strength is valuable
in stable environments and can become a liability when the environment shifts.

**Related theories.** [Organizational identity](#organizational-identity),
[Attraction-selection-attrition](#attraction-selection-attrition),
[Hofstede's cultural dimensions](#hofstede) (Section \@ref(hofstede)), [Tight and loose cultures](#tight-loose) (Section \@ref(tight-loose)),
[Institutional theory](#institutional-theory) (Section \@ref(institutional-theory)).
:::

### Core logic: Schein's three levels

@schein2010 defines culture as a pattern of shared basic assumptions that a group
has learned as it solved its problems of adapting to its environment and
integrating its members, which has worked well enough to be considered valid and
is therefore taught to new members as the correct way to perceive, think, and
feel. The definition has two important implications. Culture is **learned
history**, not management decree, and it is **deep**: its most important layer
is taken for granted and rarely discussed (Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-culture)).

```{r od-fig-culture, fig.cap = "Schein's three levels of organizational culture. Artifacts are easy to observe but hard to interpret. Basic assumptions are hard to observe but explain the levels above them. Based on Schein (2010).", fig.height = 4.6}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  A [label = "Artifacts\\nvisible structures, rituals, dress,\\noffice layout, stories, processes", %s]
  V [label = "Espoused beliefs and values\\nstated strategies, goals,\\nphilosophies, codes of conduct", %s]
  B [label = "Basic underlying assumptions\\nunconscious, taken-for-granted beliefs\\nabout reality, people, time, and work", %s]
  X [label = "Easy to see,\\nhard to decipher", %s]
  Y [label = "Hard to see,\\nultimate source of\\nvalues and action", %s]
  B -> V [label = " expressed in"]
  V -> A [label = " expressed in"]
  X -> A [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
  Y -> B [style = dotted, arrowhead = none]
  {rank = same; X; A}
  {rank = same; Y; B}
', node_outcome, node_mechanism, node_construct, node_moderator, node_moderator), rankdir = "BT", height = 440)
```

Because artifacts are ambiguous, an outsider who sees an open-plan office cannot
know whether it reflects a belief in egalitarian collaboration or simply a cost
reduction. Espoused values may also diverge from the assumptions actually in use,
the same gap Argyris and Schön identified between espoused theories and theories
in use [@argyris1978]. Schein therefore argues that culture can be diagnosed
only by probing the assumptions that make artifacts and values coherent, usually
through iterative interviews with insiders.

### Measuring culture: the Organizational Culture Profile

Quantitative research needed a way to compare cultures and to assess fit between
people and organizations. @oreilly1991 developed the **Organizational Culture
Profile (OCP)**, in which respondents sort 54 value statements according to how
characteristic they are of an organization, or how desirable they are to the
individual. Comparing the two profiles yields a measure of person-organization
fit. Factor analyses revealed dimensions such as innovation, stability, respect
for people, outcome orientation, attention to detail, team orientation, and
aggressiveness. In the original studies, person-culture fit predicted later job
satisfaction, [organizational commitment](#organizational-commitment) (Section \@ref(organizational-commitment)), and turnover. @chatman2016 argue that
the field should distinguish clearly between culture **content** (which norms)
and culture **strength** (how widely shared and intensely held), and should
connect culture explicitly to strategy.

### Evidence and extensions

The most cited quantitative finding concerns culture strength. @sorensen2002
showed that firms with strong cultures have more reliable (less variable)
performance in relatively stable environments, but that the advantage diminishes
in volatile environments, where strong cultures make it harder to detect and
respond to change. This finding connects culture to the
[exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)) tension: strong culture
supports exploitation and can impede exploration.

::: {.debate}
**Can culture be managed?** Schein treats leaders as the primary creators and
embedders of culture, especially founders. Critics from interpretive and critical
traditions argue that culture is emergent, contested, and fragmented into
subcultures, so that "managing culture" often means managing artifacts and
rhetoric rather than assumptions. A related measurement debate concerns whether
survey instruments capture culture or only climate (shared perceptions of
policies and practices). The current consensus is that both qualitative
diagnosis and quantitative profiles are needed, and that norms are best measured
by what is rewarded and sanctioned in practice [@chatman2016].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Culture integration in mergers.** Cultural incompatibility is a common
explanation for disappointing mergers. The 1998 combination of Daimler-Benz and
Chrysler, announced as a merger of equals, is a frequently cited public example:
reports of friction between German and American management styles and
decision-making norms accompanied the combined firm's difficulties, and Daimler
sold a majority of Chrysler in 2007. Because many factors affect merger
outcomes, case evidence alone cannot isolate culture. @weber2003 therefore
created cultures in the laboratory. Groups developed their own shorthand codes
for describing pictures of office scenes, and then two groups were merged.
Performance fell after the merger, participants overestimated how well the
merged group would perform, and they tended to attribute the decline to members
of the other group. The experiment shows that even trivially created cultures
generate coordination costs and attribution conflict when combined. Practical
implications include culture due diligence before a deal, explicit integration
of decision rights and vocabulary, and patience about early performance dips.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Acquisitions in which the acquirer's and target's culture profiles differ
  more will show larger post-merger turnover among target executives.
- *H2.* Culture strength will reduce performance variability more in stable than
  in volatile industries [@sorensen2002].

**Data and measures.** The OCP and its variants, employer review text (analysed
with dictionary or embedding methods for culture content), ethnography,
interviews probing assumptions, and archival indicators of rewarded behaviour.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Mistaking espoused values for culture.** Values posted on walls and websites
are espoused values. Culture lives in the assumptions that predict what people do
when values conflict or nobody is watching. A study that measures only stated
values cannot test claims about culture's effects on behaviour.
:::

## Paradox Theory {#paradox-theory}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Organizations face persistent contradictory yet interrelated
demands (for example, exploration and exploitation, control and flexibility,
global and local). Sustainable performance comes not from choosing one pole but
from accepting the tension and continually attending to both over time, a
dynamic equilibrium.

**Origins.** Organization theory. @smith2011, building on @lewis2000 and reviewed
by @schad2016.

**Level of analysis.** Individual (leaders' cognition), team, and organization.

**Key constructs.** Latent and salient tensions, paradox categories (learning,
belonging, organizing, performing), acceptance, resolution through splitting and
integration, virtuous and vicious cycles, paradoxical cognition.

**Boundary conditions.** Applies to tensions that are persistent and
interdependent. Simple trade-offs that can be resolved once by a choice are
dilemmas, not paradoxes.

**Related theories.** [Ambidexterity](#ambidexterity) (Section \@ref(ambidexterity)),
[Exploration and exploitation](#exploration-exploitation) (Section \@ref(exploration-exploitation)),
[Contingency theory](#contingency-theory) (Section \@ref(contingency-theory)).
:::

Contingency theory asks which pole of a tension fits a given environment.
Paradox theory asks how organizations can live with both. @smith2011 define
**paradox** as contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously
and persist over time. Such tensions are **latent**, embedded in organizing, and
become **salient** under conditions of **plurality** (multiple stakeholders and
views), **change**, and **scarcity** of resources. Responses that suppress one
pole (defensiveness, splitting without reconnection) produce **vicious cycles**.
Responses that combine **acceptance** of the tension with periodic, iterative
**resolution** produce **virtuous cycles** and long-term sustainability (Table \@ref(tab:od-tab-paradox)).

```{r od-tab-paradox}
tibble::tribble(
  ~`Paradox category`, ~`Underlying tension`, ~`Organizational example`,
  "Learning", "Building on the past versus destroying it to create the future", "Investing in the core product while cannibalising it with a new platform",
  "Belonging", "Identity and affiliation: the individual versus the collective, one group versus another", "Professional identities of physicians versus hospital-wide standardisation",
  "Organizing", "Structuring and leading: control versus flexibility, collaboration versus competition", "Centralised compliance controls alongside autonomous product teams",
  "Performing", "Competing goals of different stakeholders", "Social mission versus financial returns in a social enterprise"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Four categories of organizational paradox, following Smith and Lewis (2011).")
```

::: {.debate}
**Theory or vocabulary?** Paradox theory has spread rapidly, and @schad2016 warn
that the term is often used loosely for any tension or trade-off. Critics argue
that "accept and attend to both" can become unfalsifiable advice. The research
frontier focuses on precise constructs (for example, paradoxical cognition and
paradox mindset at the individual level), on the conditions under which
acceptance improves performance, and on multilevel dynamics of how tensions at
one level are managed at another.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Illustrative scenario: the social enterprise.** A microfinance organization
must serve poor borrowers (social mission) while remaining financially
self-sustaining (commercial logic). If leaders let the commercial pole dominate,
mission drift follows. If the social pole dominates, the organization runs out
of capital. A paradox approach would separate the poles structurally in some
respects (distinct metrics and governance reviews for each), integrate them
elsewhere (a board that deliberates on both at once), and revisit the balance
regularly rather than fixing it once.
:::

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Designs and measures.** Longitudinal process studies of how leaders oscillate
between poles, survey measures of paradox mindset, and comparative cases of
hybrid organizations. A testable hypothesis: leaders with higher paradoxical
cognition will sustain investment in both exploratory and exploitative projects
for longer under resource scarcity.
:::

## Psychological Safety {#psychological-safety}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Team members learn, speak up, and report errors when they share a
belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. Psychological safety
enables learning behaviour, which in turn improves team performance in
uncertain, interdependent work.

**Origins.** Organizational behaviour. @edmondson1999, drawing on @kahn1990 and
earlier work on organizational change. Reviewed by @edmondson2014 and
meta-analysed by @frazier2017.

**Level of analysis.** Team (shared climate), with individual-level variants.

**Key constructs.** Psychological safety, team learning behaviour (asking
questions, seeking feedback, discussing errors, experimenting), voice, leader
inclusiveness, status differences, accountability.

**Boundary conditions.** Matters most when work is uncertain, interdependent, and
learning-intensive. In routine, independent work, its effects on performance
are weaker.

**Related theories.** [Organizational learning](#organizational-learning),
[Leader-member exchange](#leader-member-exchange) (Section \@ref(leader-member-exchange)),
[Spiral of silence](#spiral-of-silence) (Section \@ref(spiral-of-silence)), [Groupthink](#groupthink) (Section \@ref(groupthink)),
[Transformational leadership](#transformational-leadership) (Section \@ref(transformational-leadership)).
:::

### Origins and intellectual history

The research programme started with a puzzle. In a study of hospital nursing
units, @edmondson1996 expected that better-led, better-functioning units would
make fewer medication errors. Instead, they appeared to make *more*. The
explanation was that these units were more willing to report errors, while in
units with punitive managers errors went unreported. Detected error rates partly
measured the climate for speaking up, not only the underlying frequency of
mistakes.

@edmondson1999 developed the construct of **team psychological safety**, a shared
belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking, and distinguished it
from trust (which concerns one party's expectations of another) and from
cohesiveness (which can actually suppress dissent). @kahn1990 had already
identified psychological safety as one of three conditions, together with
meaningfulness and availability, under which people bring their full selves to
work. In a multimethod field study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company,
@edmondson1999 found that psychological safety was associated with **team
learning behaviour**, which in turn was associated with team performance.

### Mechanism

Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-safety-model) shows the model of team learning.

```{r od-fig-safety-model, fig.cap = "Model of team learning. Team leader coaching and context support foster psychological safety, which enables learning behaviour and, through it, team performance. Based on Edmondson (1999)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  L [label = "Team leader coaching\\nand inclusiveness", %s]
  K [label = "Context support\\n(resources, information,\\nrewards)", %s]
  P [label = "Team psychological\\nsafety", %s]
  B [label = "Team learning behaviour\\n(asking, seeking feedback,\\ndiscussing errors)", %s]
  O [label = "Team\\nperformance", %s]
  T [label = "Task uncertainty and\\ninterdependence", %s]
  L -> P
  K -> P
  P -> B -> O
  T -> B [style = dashed]
', node_construct, node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator))
```

Psychological safety is not the same as low standards. @edmondson2018 crosses
psychological safety with performance standards to describe four zones
(Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-zones)). High safety with low standards produces a
**comfort zone**. Low safety with high standards produces an **anxiety zone**,
where people work hard but hide problems. The **learning zone** combines both.

```{r od-fig-zones, fig.cap = "Psychological safety and performance standards: four zones. Stylised teams are plotted for illustration. Framework based on Edmondson (2018).", fig.height = 4.6}
set.seed(2018)
teams <- data.frame(safety = runif(40, 0.05, 0.95), standards = runif(40, 0.05, 0.95))
zones <- data.frame(
  x = c(0.25, 0.75, 0.25, 0.75), y = c(0.25, 0.25, 0.75, 0.75),
  lab = c("Apathy zone", "Comfort zone", "Anxiety zone", "Learning zone")
)
ggplot(teams, aes(safety, standards)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0.5, xmax = 1, ymin = 0.5, ymax = 1, fill = pal[["aqua"]], alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(colour = pal[["blue"]], alpha = 0.55, size = 2) +
  geom_label(data = zones, aes(x, y, label = lab), size = 3.8, fontface = "bold",
             colour = ink[["primary"]], fill = "white", label.size = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0.1, 0.9), labels = c("Low", "High")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), breaks = c(0.1, 0.9), labels = c("Low", "High")) +
  labs(x = "Psychological safety", y = "Performance standards (motivation and accountability)",
       title = "Safety without standards is comfort, standards without safety is anxiety",
       caption = "Stylised teams (illustrative). Quadrant labels follow Edmondson (2018).")
```

### Evidence and extensions

The construct has a large and broadly consistent evidence base. @frazier2017
meta-analysed research on psychological safety and found it positively related
to information sharing, learning behaviour, engagement, and task performance,
with supportive leadership and peer relationships among its antecedents. In
healthcare, @nembhard2006 studied neonatal intensive care unit teams and found
that lower-status professionals felt less psychologically safe than physicians,
but that **leader inclusiveness** (words and deeds by leaders that invite and
appreciate others' contributions) raised psychological safety and weakened the
status gap. @edmondson2001 showed that surgical teams that successfully adopted a
new cardiac procedure were those whose leaders framed the change as a team
learning challenge and made it safe for nurses and technicians to speak up.
@edmondson2014 review the construct's history and its extension from teams to
organizations and to topics such as innovation, voice, and safety.

::: {.debate}
**Climate, trait, or fad?** Three critiques recur. First, measurement: the
standard seven-item scale is a perception measure, and aggregating it to the team
level requires evidence of within-team agreement. Second, causality: most studies
are cross-sectional, so high-performing teams may feel safe because they perform
well. Third, popularization: in practitioner discourse, psychological safety is
sometimes equated with comfort or the absence of criticism, which is close to
the opposite of the construct. Edmondson's own framing pairs safety with high
standards and candour [@edmondson2018].
:::

### Applications in business

::: {.business-case}
**Hospitals and tech teams.** Healthcare offers the clearest evidence that
speaking up saves lives and money. Checklists, structured briefings, and
practices that let any team member stop a procedure are institutional designs
for psychological safety, and the research above shows that leader behaviour
determines whether they are used [@nembhard2006; @edmondson2001]. In technology,
Google's internal research project on team effectiveness, known as Project
Aristotle, became widely publicised in 2015 and 2016. Google reported that
psychological safety was the most important of five dynamics that distinguished
effective teams, alongside dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and
impact [@duhigg2016]. Blameless post-incident reviews, common in site reliability
engineering, apply the same logic: they focus on systemic causes so that
engineers disclose what actually happened.
:::

### Using the theory in research

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Sample hypotheses.**

- *H1.* Team psychological safety will be positively related to the number of
  near misses reported, controlling for workload.
- *H2.* Leader inclusiveness will weaken the negative relationship between
  professional status and individual psychological safety [@nembhard2006].
- *H3.* The effect of psychological safety on team performance will be stronger
  for teams with high task uncertainty.

**Measures.** Edmondson's team psychological safety scale aggregated to the team
level after checking agreement indices, behavioural measures of voice and error
reporting, and observational coding of meetings.

**Designs.** Multilevel field surveys, longitudinal panels to address reverse
causality, and field experiments with leader training or structured debriefs.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Confusing safety with comfort.** Psychological safety is about the freedom to
take interpersonal risks such as admitting mistakes and challenging ideas, not
about being shielded from disagreement or accountability. Interventions that
reduce candour in the name of "safety" undermine the mechanism the theory
describes.
:::

## Attraction-Selection-Attrition {#attraction-selection-attrition}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** People are attracted to organizations whose members resemble
them, are selected by organizations that prefer people who fit, and leave when
they do not fit. Over time the cycle makes organizations increasingly
homogeneous, and that homogeneity, not formal structure, defines the place.

**Origins.** Industrial and organizational psychology. @schneider1987, updated in
@schneider1995.

**Level of analysis.** Individual and organization.

**Key constructs.** Attraction, selection, attrition, homogeneity, person-organization
fit, founder influence.

**Boundary conditions.** Requires voluntary labour mobility and discretion in
selection. Weaker in tight labour markets or under strict diversity mandates.

**Related theories.** [Person-environment fit](#person-environment-fit) (Section \@ref(person-environment-fit)),
[Organizational culture](#organizational-culture), [Homophily](#homophily) (Section \@ref(homophily)).
:::

@schneider1987 argued, in a paper titled "The people make the place", that
organizational behaviour should be explained by the characteristics of the
people in the organization rather than by structures and technologies alone.
Founders' personalities shape early goals and hiring. Applicants who share those
values find the organization attractive. Recruiters select people who seem to
fit. Employees who do not fit leave. The **homogeneity hypothesis** follows:
organizations become more homogeneous in personality and values over time. This
helps explain why cultures persist [@schneider1995] and links the theory to
person-organization fit research [@chatman1989; @kristof1996; @oreilly1991].
Figure \@ref(fig:od-fig-asa) simulates the process.

```{r od-fig-asa, fig.cap = "Illustrative simulation of the attraction-selection-attrition cycle. Under ASA, applicants and leavers are filtered by distance from the founder's values and the spread of values shrinks. With fit-neutral hiring, diversity is maintained. Stylised data.", fig.height = 4}
set.seed(1987)
simulate_asa <- function(asa = TRUE, years = 20, n = 200) {
  v <- rnorm(n, 0, 1)                                             # employees' values (founder = 0)
  out <- numeric(years)
  for (t in 1:years) {
    p_leave <- if (asa) plogis(-3 + 1.2 * abs(v)) else rep(plogis(-3 + 1.2 * 0.8), n)
    v <- v[runif(length(v)) > p_leave]                             # attrition
    pool <- rnorm(600, 0, 1)                                       # labour market
    if (asa) pool <- pool[runif(600) < plogis(1 - 1.5 * abs(pool))] # attraction
    need <- n - length(v)
    hires <- if (asa) pool[order(abs(pool))][seq_len(need)] else sample(pool, need)  # selection
    v <- c(v, hires)
    out[t] <- sd(v)
  }
  out
}
asa <- bind_rows(
  data.frame(year = 1:20, sd = simulate_asa(TRUE), regime = "ASA cycle (fit-based attraction, selection, attrition)"),
  data.frame(year = 1:20, sd = simulate_asa(FALSE), regime = "Fit-neutral hiring and turnover")
)
ggplot(asa, aes(year, sd, colour = regime)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]])) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1.2)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Spread of employee values (SD)", colour = NULL,
       title = "The people make the place, and the place selects the people",
       caption = "Stylised agent simulation (n = 200 employees, founder values = 0).")
```

::: {.debate}
**Homogeneity: asset or liability?** Homogeneity eases coordination and supports
a strong culture, but Schneider himself warned that it can make organizations
unable to perceive or adapt to environmental change. Empirical support for
organization-level homogeneity in personality is moderate, and critics note that
job and occupational requirements also produce similarity. The theory also sits
uneasily with diversity goals: "cultural fit" in hiring can become a vehicle for
similarity bias.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Hiring for culture fit or culture add.** Many technology firms once screened
explicitly for "culture fit", and some have publicly reframed the criterion as
"culture add" or values alignment, precisely to avoid the homogenising spiral that
